title: Conductance of silicon nanotube junctions in high magnetic fields
authors: Teresa Kulka, Juan Alberto Canché-Martín, Irina V. Lebedeva, Jacek A. Majewski, Karolina Z. Milowska
abstract: We investigate coherent quantum transport through silicon nanotube (SiNT) junctions in high magnetic fields up to 60 T using a tight-binding model combined with the non-equilibrium Green's function formalism, and magnetic field included via Peierls substitution. We consider junctions of metallic nanotubes (6,0)+(6,0) and semiconducting ones (9,9)+(9,9), and examine the effects of the overlap length, inter-tube distance, magnetic-field direction, and field strength on the electronic transmission. In contrast to carbon nanotube junctions, the SiNT systems exhibit irregular transmission oscillations and do not show the emergence of highly conductive gateway states. The transmission is substantially more sensitive to a magnetic field perpendicular to the nanotube axis than to a parallel field, while increasing the field strength progressively modifies the transmission spectrum. Increasing the overlap length results in more frequent transmission oscillations, whereas increasing the inter-tube distance modifies their positions and amplitudes without changing their overall character. Generally, similar trends are observed for both types of junctions, involving metallic and semiconducting nanotubes. However, in the junction of semiconducting nanotubes, one observes peculiar additional field-dependent in-gap transmission features. These results demonstrate that the magnetic-field response of SiNT junctions is strongly governed by their geometry and differs qualitatively from that of pristine carbon nanotube junctions.
summary: This theoretical study characterizes the quantum electronic transport through silicon nanotube junctions under strong magnetic fields. Using a tight-binding model and NEGF formalism, the authors find that the magnetic response is highly sensitive to the field's orientation and junction geometry. The results establish unique magnetotransport signatures for SiNTs, distinguishing them from carbon nanotubes.
main_problem: The study investigates coherent quantum transport through silicon nanotube (SiNT) junctions when subjected to high external magnetic fields.
main_result: SiNT junctions exhibit irregular transmission oscillations, are highly sensitive to magnetic fields perpendicular to the tube axis, and show distinct field-dependent in-gap features in semiconducting junctions, differing significantly from carbon nanotube behavior.
method: The research employs a tight-binding (TB) model solved using the Non-Equilibrium Green's Function (NEGF) formalism, incorporating magnetic fields via the Peierls substitution.
model_or_system: The system consists of SiNT junctions, modeled using a four-orbital tight-binding Hamiltonian derived from DFT calculations. The junctions studied are metallic (6,0)+(6,0) and semiconducting (9,9)+(9,9) types.
key_observables: Electronic transmission spectrum T(E), oscillation frequency, and the presence/absence of in-gap transmission features.
important_parameters: Magnetic field strength up to 60 T, magnetic field direction (perpendicular vs. parallel to the axis), overlap length, and inter-tube distance.
main_assumptions: The Zeeman contribution is neglected, focusing solely on the orbital response to the magnetic field. TB parameters are fitted to initial DFT results.
figures_summary: Figures show band structures comparing TB to DFT for both junction types, and transmission spectra illustrating the dependence on overlap length, inter-tube distance, and applied magnetic field strength.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of establishing the physical model (DFT/TB parametrization), applying the NEGF formalism to calculate magnetotransport, and systematically analyzing the results based on junction geometry and field orientation.
why_interesting: The detailed study of magnetotransport in semiconductor nanostructures provides a platform to test theoretical models of quantum confinement and orbital coupling in low-dimensional systems, which has parallels with superconducting or quantum wire physics.
